title: ES₅ as a sandpile-group pairing condition on a 4-vertex fan multigraph
connection: The chain matrix M = [[v,−1,0],[−1,t,−1],[0,−1,u]] is the reduced Laplacian of the multigraph: path a–b–c plus a sink s joined to a, b, c by v−1, t−2, u−1 parallel edges. It has det M = tuv−u−v = p spanning trees, a cyclic sandpile group ℤ/p, and its discriminant (monodromy) pairing has self-pairing (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) (∃ t,u,v ≥ 2, tuv−u−v = p, (A/p) = −1 with A = tu−1; sufficient for ES(p)) ⇔ some fan multigraph of this shape with p spanning trees has a sandpile pairing in the non-square class.
why: Sandpile groups with their pairings are a mature field (Lorenzini, Shokrieh, Bosch–Lorenzini) with classification results for pairings on cyclic critical groups; this gives ES₅ a purely graph-theoretic statement.
first_step: Script: for p ≡ 1 (4) < 10⁵, enumerate all graphs on ≤ 5 vertices with p spanning trees and record which pairing classes occur; is the non-square class reached by 4-vertex fans exactly when ES₅(p) holds, and always by 5-vertex graphs?
refs: arXiv:2311.06367 (Lorenzini, The critical polynomial of a graph)

title: Relaxing the fan: which pairing classes occur among graphs with p spanning trees and k vertices
connection: Generalise item 1: the graph-theoretic analogue of 'ES with more terms' is 'some graph with ≤ k vertices and τ(G) = p has a non-square sandpile pairing'. For k large this is trivially true (cycles/paths); ES₅ is the k = 4 fan case.
why: Gives a ladder of relaxations parametrised by vertex count, with a known extremal theory for τ(G) values (Sedláček's α(n)); the threshold k(p) at which the non-square pairing first appears is a new invariant to compare with λ(p).
first_step: Compute k*(p) = least vertex count with a non-square pairing and τ = p, for p < 10⁴; compare with λ(p) and with Stong/Azarija–Škrekovski bounds for α(p).
refs: Stong, Minimal graphs with a prescribed number of spanning trees, Australas. J. Combin. 82 (2022)

title: Spanning-tree values and Zaremba (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak) applied to fan graphs
connection: Chan–Kontorovich–Pak prove exponential growth of the set of spanning-tree counts of n-vertex planar graphs via continued fractions, thin orbits and Zaremba. ES₅ asks the same kind of question for continuants of length 3 with a sign condition.
why: It is the nearest proved theorem in which spanning-tree counts and continued fractions are linked through thin-orbit methods. Their graphs realise numerators of CFs, as our fan does for HJ length 3.
first_step: Read arXiv:2411.18782 §2 (graph ↔ CF dictionary). Check whether their construction realises a prescribed numerator p with a prescribed denominator class (A/p) = −1 at bounded length.
refs: arXiv:2411.18782 (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak, Spanning trees and continued fractions)

title: Modular spanning-tree realisation (Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner) as a model for the sign condition
connection: Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner show every residue u mod N is τ(G) mod N for some planar G on O(log N) vertices. ES₅ is a 'τ(G) = p exactly and pairing class prescribed' statement on 4 vertices.
why: Their short combinatorial proofs control τ(G) modulo N with few vertices; a version controlling the pairing class (a mod-p quadratic datum) would be a graph-theoretic analogue of an ES-type sign theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2503.23648; check whether their gadgets allow simultaneous control of τ(G) and the square class of the sandpile pairing.

title: Idoneal numbers in spanning-tree extremal problems vs U(n)/I3 sporadic lists
connection: Azarija–Škrekovski: α(n) ≤ (n+4)/3 iff n ∉ {3,4,5,6,7,9,10,13,18,22}, a subset of Euler's idoneal numbers. U(n)/I3 have finite sporadic failure lists for tuv−u−v representations, also continuant/spanning-tree statements.
why: The appearance of idoneal numbers (class-group exponent ≤ 2) in a spanning-tree problem suggests the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} might have a class-group characterisation.
first_step: Compute the class groups Cl(−4n), Cl(−n) for the U(n) sporadics and for I3 failures; test exponent-2 / genus-one patterns.

title: Effective resistance A/p of a 3-node ladder network
connection: In the fan network with unit conductances, the effective resistance between a and the sink is (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) ⇔ a three-node ladder network with integer conductances to ground and total 'tree count' p has R_eff(a,s) = A/p with A a non-residue mod p.
why: Electrical-network theory has exact theorems on which rationals are resistances of networks with k unit resistors (series–parallel ↔ continued fractions). The ES sign becomes a residuosity property of a physical quantity.
first_step: Enumerate rational resistances of networks with ≤ 12 unit resistors (OEIS A048211 family); check whether non-residue numerators A/p appear at small resistor counts for every p ≡ 1 (4) < 2000.

title: Lens space L(p,A) not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1), bounding a 3-chain plumbing
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] means L(p,A) bounds the linear plumbing with Euler numbers −v,−t,−u. Whitehead: L(p,q) ≃ L(p,q′) iff qq′ ≡ ±m² (mod p). For p ≡ 1 (4) prime, (A/p) = −1 ⇔ L(p,A) ≄ L(p,1). So ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space of order p that is not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1) bounds a negative-definite linear plumbing with 3 vertices.
why: Turns ES₅ into a 3-manifold statement about the 'plumbing length' of homotopy types, where the homotopy type is the ES sign.
first_step: Tabulate min plumbing length over the non-L(p,1) homotopy class for p < 10⁵ (= λ(p)); look for 4-manifold invariants (d-invariants, Casson–Walker) that bound plumbing length from above.

title: Linking form of the double branched cover of a 2-bridge link with 3 twist regions
connection: L(p,A) is the double branched cover of the 2-bridge link b(p,A). The ES₅ sign is the isometry class of the linking form of Σ₂(b(p,A)), and HJ length 3 means a 3-term even-CF (plumbing/Goeritz) description of the 2-bridge knot.
why: Knot theory has exact formulas tying linking forms, Goeritz matrices and signatures (Gordon–Litherland). If σ mod 8 detects (A/p), the ES sign becomes a knot signature on a 3-parameter knot family.
first_step: Compute σ(b(p,A)) by Murasugi's formula Σ_{i<p} (−1)^{⌊iA/p⌋} for p < 500. Check whether σ mod 8, together with p mod 8, determines (A/p) (a van der Blij / Gauss-sum reciprocity).
refs: Gordon–Litherland 1978, On the signature of a link

title: Heegaard Floer d-invariants of L(p,A) as an obstruction/selector for 3-chain plumbings
connection: d-invariants of lens spaces satisfy an explicit recursion (Ozsváth–Szabó), d(L(p,q),i) via d(L(q, p mod q), j). Plumbing length 3 constrains the negative-definite fillings, and the ES sign is the homotopy class.
why: d-invariants are the native tool for deciding which lens spaces bound which definite 4-manifolds (Lisca's rational-ball classification used them). They might give a closed-form test of 'some 3-chain filling exists in the non-square class'.
first_step: Implement the Ozsváth–Szabó recursion. For p < 2000, compare Σ_i d(L(p,A),i) statistics over the classes A with r(p/A) = 3 between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Casson–Walker invariant / Dedekind sum of L(p,A) restricted to HJ-length-3 A
connection: λ_CW(L(p,q)) is a Dedekind sum s(q,p) up to normalisation, and Rademacher-type congruences tie 12p·s(q,p) mod 8 to (q/p). On words, s(A,p) has a closed form in (t,u,v) by Dedekind reciprocity.
why: It gives an explicit integer-valued topological invariant of the word whose residue mod 8 is the ES sign. Sums over words then become sums of a topological invariant.
first_step: Derive s(tu−1, p) in closed form from three applications of reciprocity; compare with DEDEKIND_ES §4.

title: Rational balls bounded by lens spaces (Lisca) vs 3-chain plumbings
connection: Lisca classified lens spaces bounding rational homology balls (p = m², specific q). Square p is exactly where ES-type certificates vanish (T1), and rational-ball bounding is tied to the linking form being metabolic.
why: T1 (obstruction at odd squares) and 'bounds a rational ball' are both 'linking form is split/hyperbolic' phenomena. A Lisca-style lattice-embedding argument could explain T1 topologically and show why primes escape it.
first_step: Read Lisca math/0701610 §§2–3 (lattice embeddings). Check whether the T1 square-class obstruction is equivalent to the metabolic linking form of L(m², A) for the relevant A.
refs: arXiv:math/0701610 (Lisca, Lens spaces, rational balls and the ribbon conjecture)

title: Lattice embedding of the 3-chain into the diagonal lattice ℤ^k (Donaldson-style)
connection: Donaldson's theorem forces definite fillings to embed their intersection lattice in −ℤ^k. For the chain (v,t,u), embeddings into ℤ^3 or ℤ^4 are explicit combinatorics, and the ES sign is a property of the complement lattice's discriminant.
why: This is the native toolbox of 4-dimensional topology for lens spaces, and it turns ES₅ into a finite combinatorial embedding question at each p.
first_step: Enumerate embeddings of chain lattices with det p into ℤ⁴ for p < 500; check whether the orthogonal complement's discriminant square class equals the ES sign.

title: Cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A) with a 3-curve resolution and non-residue A
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] is the minimal resolution chain (−v,−t,−u) of the cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A). ES₅(p) ⇔ some 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has exactly 3 exceptional curves.
why: Singularity theory controls resolution lengths via Riemenschneider duality, P-resolutions and smoothing components (KSB). The ES sign is a Galois-type datum: is 1/p(1,A) isomorphic over a quadratic twist to 1/p(1,1)?
first_step: Compute embedding dimension and Riemenschneider dual lengths for A ∈ L₃(p); test whether the dual-chain length distribution differs between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Kollár–Shepherd-Barron P-resolutions and Wahl singularities 1/m²(1, ma−1) as the T1 locus
connection: Wahl (T-)singularities 1/(dm²)(1, dma−1) have rational-ball (QHD) smoothings and sit at square orders, exactly where T1 kills certificates. KSB P-resolutions of 1/p(1,A) are counted by zero continued fractions.
why: The T1 obstruction may be the shadow of 'square-order cyclic quotients admit QHD smoothings'. Smoothing theory would then give a geometric reason for the square/prime dichotomy.
first_step: Compute, for A ∈ L₃(m²), whether 1/m²(1,A) is a Wahl singularity or admits a QHD smoothing, and compare with the T1 certificate emptiness.

title: Hacking–Prokhorov degenerations of P² to P(a²,b²,c²) and Markov-type equations for ES
connection: Hacking–Prokhorov: toric degenerations of P² to weighted projective planes with T-singularities are governed by Markov triples a²+b²+c² = 3abc, generated by mutations. ES's Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: nA²+B²+D = ABC is a twisted analogue.
why: Mutation trees of degenerations give an infinite combinatorial structure over a Markov-type equation, and the ES surfaces lack exactly such a mutation structure (only coordinate permutations). This is a place to look for a hidden mutation.
first_step: Check whether S_{n,D} solutions arise as weights of Q-Gorenstein degenerations of some del Pezzo (degree depending on n); start from HP's classification table.

title: Toric surface with three boundary curves: HJ-length-3 cones as compact toric surface data
connection: A 2-dim cone of type 1/p(1,A) whose resolution has 3 rays corresponds to a toric surface patch. ES₅ asks for a smooth fan refinement with 3 new rays whose self-intersections (−v,−t,−u) give p, with a twist class.
why: Toric geometry turns the condition into lattice-polygon combinatorics (Oda's 12/24 theorem for complete fans), which might give global constraints linking different A's.
first_step: Write the 3-ray refinement condition as a lattice-polygon statement; check whether completing the fan to a compact toric surface forces relations between v, t, u and A (mod 4).
refs: Oda, Convex bodies and algebraic geometry (1988)

title: Tridiagonal ternary lattice of determinant p in the non-square genus
connection: The Gram matrix M(t,u,v) defines a positive definite ternary lattice of determinant p with basis e₁,e₂,e₃, e₁·e₃ = 0, e₁·e₂ = e₂·e₃ = −1. Its discriminant form is A/p on ℤ/p. ES₅(p) ⇔ the genus of ternary lattices of det p with non-square discriminant form contains a lattice admitting such a chain basis with norms ≥ 2.
why: This is the native language of ternary quadratic forms: genus/class tables (Brandt–Intrau), Siegel mass, and representation of binary sublattices. It brings Duke–Schulze-Pillot style tools.
first_step: For p < 2000, list the reduced ternary forms of det p in each genus (Eisenstein reduction). Count the classes admitting a chain basis, and check whether the non-square genus always has one iff ES₅(p).

title: Chain basis ⇔ representation of the binary lattice [[v,−1],[−1,t]] with a prescribed orthogonal vector
connection: A chain basis exists iff the ternary lattice L contains a primitive binary sublattice ≅ [[v,−1],[−1,t]] whose orthogonal complement direction meets L appropriately. This is a 'representation of binary forms by ternary forms' problem with an extra condition.
why: Representation of binary forms by ternary/quaternary forms has deep equidistribution results (Ellenberg–Venkatesh; Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh). These give existence for large discriminant, but with growing discriminant here.
first_step: Formulate: for each binary form b of disc ≈ 4tv−4 ≤ X, is b represented by a ternary of det p in the non-square genus with the extra e₃ condition? Compare with the Ellenberg–Venkatesh hypotheses.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Local-global principles for representations of quadratic forms (Invent. 2008)

title: Frobenius-class form: uv | n+u+v ⇔ n is in the 'Frobenius shadow' of the numerical semigroup ⟨u,v⟩
connection: n = tuv−u−v ⇔ n ≡ −(u+v) (mod uv). By Popoviciu's formula, n then has exactly t−1 representations as au+bv (a,b ≥ 0); n = uv−u−v is the Frobenius number. ES₅ words are pairs (u,v) whose denumerant at n is in the Frobenius residue class, plus a sign condition.
why: The theory of numerical semigroups and denumerants (Popoviciu, Sylvester, Ramírez Alfonsín) gives a new vocabulary for the forest F_p (uv | p+u+v), with generating-function tools.
first_step: Express the ES₅ sign in terms of (u,v,n) via denumerant data; check whether Σ_{(u,v)} sign·q^n has a Popoviciu-type generating function (∏ 1/(1−q^u)(1−q^v) restricted to a class).
refs: Ramírez Alfonsín, The Diophantine Frobenius Problem (2005)

title: Sylver coinage / numerical-semigroup games on the forest's Frobenius classes
connection: The forest edge relation uv | p+u+v identifies p as a 'Frobenius-shadow' point of ⟨u,v⟩. Conway's Sylver coinage is a game whose positions are numerical semigroups; P-positions are related to Frobenius data.
why: Game positions give a different combinatorial calculus on pairs (u,v); an ES-relevant invariant might appear as a Sprague–Grundy value. Low prior but not meaningless.
first_step: Compute Sprague–Grundy-type data for two-generator Sylver positions ⟨u,v⟩ with uv | p+u+v; look for any correlation with (uv/p).

title: Christoffel/Sturmian word of slope A/p with three runs
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is a run-length statistic of the Christoffel word of slope A/p (equivalently the cutting sequence of the segment to (p,A)). ES₅ asks for a non-residue A whose Christoffel word has the minimal 3-block structure.
why: Combinatorics on words has exact results on Christoffel words, palindromes and standard factorizations, which might give explicit constructions of A with prescribed structure, for instance via palindromic closure.
first_step: Express r(p/A) = 3 as a factorisation condition on the Christoffel word; test whether the Lothaire standard factorisation relates the two halves to (A/p).
refs: Lothaire, Algebraic Combinatorics on Words, ch. 2

title: Goeritz matrix of an alternating 2-bridge diagram equals the chain matrix
connection: For the plumbing description, the Goeritz form of a 2-bridge link diagram is (up to sign and stabilisation) the tridiagonal chain matrix. Gordon–Litherland gives σ = sign(G) − μ.
why: This pins ES₅ to an explicit knot diagram: a 3-twist-region 2-bridge knot of determinant p. Knot tables could be scanned for the sign.
first_step: Check against KnotInfo: for 2-bridge knots with det p ≡ 1 (4), p < 200, and 3 twist regions in even CF form, record the linking-form class.

title: Quantum (WRT) invariants of lens spaces: Gauss sums carrying (A/p)
connection: Jeffrey's formula for the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of L(p,q) involves Dedekind sums and quadratic Gauss sums whose evaluation produces Jacobi symbols in q. The ES sign may appear as a phase of a quantum invariant of L(p,A).
why: Quantum topology has exact formulas (and quantum modularity results) for WRT invariants of Seifert/lens spaces. A sum over words of a quantum invariant could be a computable object.
first_step: Write τ_r(L(p,A)) (Jeffrey 1992). Check whether some level r makes the phase equal to (A/p), and evaluate Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p)} τ_r(L(p,A)).
refs: L. Jeffrey, Chern–Simons–Witten invariants of lens spaces and torus bundles (CMP 1992)

title: Plumbing calculus moves (blow-up/blow-down of ±1 curves) as certificate transport
connection: Kirby calculus moves change a plumbing chain without changing the boundary lens space. The boundary words (letters = 1) of LENGTH_THREE are formal words that become interior after blow-downs.
why: This gives a topological interpretation of the repo's boundary/interior word distinction and of 'transport' moves between certificates at different n (via ±1 blow-ups changing the plumbing's det).
first_step: Map LENGTH_THREE formal words (letter 1) to blow-down sequences; check whether ES transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md) are Kirby moves.

title: Seifert fibred spaces with three exceptional fibres and orbifold base S²(x,y,z)
connection: ES's own form 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n is an orbifold Euler characteristic statement χ(S²(x,y,z)) = 4/n − 1. Seifert spaces over S²(x,y,z) with Euler number e have |H₁| = xyz·|e| (for suitable normalisation), so ES is a statement about which Seifert invariants give prescribed rational χ.
why: This translates ES into 3-manifold language unrelated to the HJ chain: the original equation becomes a geometric (orbifold) invariant, and the field knows χ-spectra of orbifolds.
first_step: Write H₁ and χ for Seifert spaces M(0; (x,β₁),(y,β₂),(z,β₃)); check whether ES(n) is equivalent to the existence of one with χ = 4/n − 1 and an extra homological condition with natural meaning (e.g. |H₁| ≡ 0 mod n).

title: Triangle groups of covolume 2π(1 − 4/n)
connection: ES(n) for n ≥ 5 ⇔ there is a hyperbolic triangle group Δ(x,y,z) whose orbifold area is 2π(1 − 4/n), equivalently a hyperbolic triangle with angles π/x, π/y, π/z and area π(n−4)/n.
why: The covolume spectrum of Fuchsian groups is classically studied (Siegel's minimal covolume, signature theory). ES becomes 'every number of the form 2π(n−4)/n is a triangle-group covolume'.
first_step: Search the literature for results on the set of covolumes of triangle groups, e.g. 'which rationals are 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z'; check whether any density/representation theorem exists.

title: Hyperbolic triangle billiards / Veech triangles with prescribed area
connection: Billiards in the (π/x, π/y, π/z) triangle unfold to translation surfaces. Veech's lattice triangles are special triangle shapes. ES is a statement about the area spectrum of reflection-group triangles.
why: A genuine dynamics translation of the original equation, but probably only a restatement. Recorded for breadth.
first_step: Check whether the area/angle condition has any known role in Veech-group classification (Kenyon–Smillie, Ward triangles).

title: Triangles with integer exradii and inradius n/4
connection: For any triangle 1/r = 1/r_a + 1/r_b + 1/r_c, and every positive triple (r_a,r_b,r_c) is realised by a unique triangle (Ravi substitution). So ES(n) ⇔ there is a triangle with integer exradii and inradius exactly n/4.
why: An exact, unrestricted Euclidean-geometry form. Triangle geometry has its own integrality theory (Heronian triangles, integer exradii), and a Heronian strengthening gives testable variants.
first_step: Test the stronger variant 'exists a Heronian triangle with integer exradii and inradius n/4' for n ≤ 10⁴; if it holds broadly, rational parametrisations of Heronian triangles give new families.

title: Triangles with integer altitudes and inradius n/4 (the x > n/2 subfamily)
connection: 1/h_a + 1/h_b + 1/h_c = 1/r. A triangle with altitudes x,y,z exists iff the reciprocals satisfy the triangle inequality, i.e. iff x > n/2 for the smallest x. So 'ES with x ∈ (n/2, 3n/4]' ⇔ a triangle with integer altitudes and inradius n/4.
why: It is a natural geometric sub-variant whose truth or falsity is unknown. If it is true for all primes, it is a stronger statement with more geometric structure.
first_step: Compute, for primes p ≤ 10⁶, whether an ES solution with p/2 < x ≤ 3p/4 exists; list the failures.

title: Thin-lens / parallel-resistor restatement: three integer elements combining to n/4
connection: Three resistors x,y,z in parallel give n/4. Three thin lenses in contact with focal lengths x,y,z give focal length n/4.
why: This is a pure restatement, but physical intuition (series–parallel networks ↔ continued fractions) connects to the HJ form. Recorded once for completeness.
first_step: None beyond item 6 (resistor networks); use as a pedagogical bridge only.

title: Kirchhoff/Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: squared rectangles from planar networks with p spanning trees
connection: A planar network with τ = p spanning trees gives a rectangle tiled by squares with sides of total scale p (BSST). The fan graph of item 1 is planar, so ES₅ gives a squared rectangle of a specific shape whose aspect ratio encodes the resistance A/p.
why: Squared-rectangle theory has a 'reduced side' (= τ) and aspect ratios = resistances. ES₅ becomes: some 4-vertex-network squared rectangle with reduced side p has aspect class non-residue.
first_step: Compute BSST rectangles for the fan networks at small p; check whether the aspect-ratio numerator class is visible geometrically (e.g. via tile parity).

title: Domino/strip tilings counted by continuants with a parity weight
connection: Positive continuants count tilings of a strip by monominoes and dominoes with weights. The negative continuant K(v,t,u) = tuv−u−v is a signed count, equivalently det of the chain matrix as a weighted path-matching count. The ES sign is the class of the cofactor.
why: Tiling enumeration has transfer-matrix and involution machinery. A sign-reversing involution on tilings might isolate a non-residue cofactor.
first_step: Write tuv−u−v and tu−1 as tiling counts of a 3-cell strip with weights; look for a sign-reversing involution whose fixed points carry the class of tu−1 mod p.
refs: Benjamin–Quinn, Proofs that Really Count (continuants ch. 4)

title: Matrix-tree theorem with signed/twisted weights: the ES sign as a determinant of a twisted Laplacian
connection: (A/p) for the fan graph equals the Legendre symbol of a principal cofactor of the Laplacian. Twisted Laplacians (connection Laplacians with ℤ/2 or ℤ/4 holonomy) compute signed spanning-forest counts (Kenyon's cycle-rooted spanning forests).
why: Kenyon's vector-bundle Laplacian theory computes topological invariants of forests via determinants. A ℤ/4 connection might encode the slot-lemma condition '4 | some pentagon entry'.
first_step: Put a ℤ/4 connection on the fan graph; compute det of the connection Laplacian and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all words for p < 1000.
refs: Kenyon, Spanning forests and the vector bundle Laplacian (Ann. Probab. 2011)

title: Hoffman/spectral bound on the forest F_p with Legendre colouring (bichromatic edge existence)
connection: ES₅ for p ≡ 1 (8) ⇔ the word forest F_p has a bichromatic edge under v ↦ (v/p). Spectral graph theory bounds the size of monochromatic (independent-type) sets via eigenvalues.
why: It is the textbook first tool for 'every 2-colouring with given class sizes has a bichromatic edge'. The Legendre colouring has known sizes inside intervals (Burgess), but F_p is sparse.
first_step: Compute the spectrum of F_p for p < 10⁴; compare λ_max/λ_min with the size of the QR set inside vertices to see if Hoffman-type bounds are anywhere near.

title: Isoperimetry/expansion of the forest components vs character-sum smoothness
connection: If the component of 1 in F_p has edge expansion h and contains a QNR, then a bichromatic edge exists. Combinatorial expansion of an arithmetic forest is a graph-theory question.
why: It reduces ES₅ to 'the component containing 1 reaches a QNR', the arithmetic analogue of a percolation/connectivity statement.
first_step: Compute the component sizes of F_p and the least QNR inside the component of 1, for p < 10⁶.

title: Ising model on F_p: ES₅ failure = zero-energy configuration of a frustrated ferromagnet
connection: Put spins σ_v = (v/p) on F_p. ES₅ failure (no bichromatic edge) means the Legendre configuration is a ground state of the ferromagnetic Ising Hamiltonian on F_p. Statistical mechanics has Peierls/contour arguments for when ground states must have domain walls.
why: A Peierls-type argument combines an 'external field' (Legendre symbol bias on short intervals) with graph connectivity. It is a native tool not obviously tried.
first_step: Compute, per component of F_p, the fraction of +spins; check whether components are ever large and monochromatic (they cannot be if ES₅ holds).

title: Critical group (sandpile) of F_p itself
connection: Beyond the 4-vertex fan per word, the whole forest F_p (vertices 1..p+2) is a graph whose Laplacian/critical group might carry p-arithmetic.
why: Speculative: if F_p's structure (degrees = numbers of divisors in classes) gives a critical group with a p-part, Lorenzini pairings might see the Legendre colouring globally.
first_step: Compute the Smith normal form of the Laplacian of F_p for p < 2000; look for p-torsion or Legendre-related invariants.

title: Farey-graph geodesic of length 3 in the non-residue class
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is (up to normalisation) a combinatorial distance-type statistic in the Farey graph from ∞ to p/A via a specific path type. ES₅ asks whether the Farey ball of 'HJ radius 3' around ∞ contains a vertex p/A with A a QNR.
why: The Farey graph is hyperbolic geometry's combinatorial skeleton, and its metric theory (Beardon–Hockman–Short) is well developed.
first_step: Compare r(p/A) with Farey distance d(∞, p/A) for p < 10⁴; check whether the ES₅ condition is a Farey-distance condition for a known metric.

title: Ford circles: A/p lies in a horoball of 'depth-3' chain
connection: r(p/A) = 3 means the Ford circle chain from ∞ to A/p has three tangency steps of HJ type. ES₅ becomes: some non-residue A has A/p inside the union of depth-3 Ford horoball chains.
why: The Ford circle picture makes the condition a covering-by-horoballs statement, where hyperbolic volume arguments live.
first_step: Draw/compute the union of depth-3 HJ horoball chains intersected with {A/p}; measure its proportion and its correlation with QR.

title: Closed horocycle of period p: depth-3 cusp excursion at a non-residue point
connection: The points (A/p + i/p) for A ∈ (ℤ/p)^× form the closed horocycle of length p on SL₂(ℤ)\H. Small HJ length means the corresponding geodesic/horocycle point enters the cusp in a prescribed pattern; ES₅ asks for a QNR point with a 3-step pattern.
why: Equidistribution of closed horocycles with twists by characters (Sarnak, Strömbergsson, Venkatesh's sparse equidistribution) is a native toolbox. ES needs extreme cusp events, which are small-measure.
first_step: Compute the measure of the 'HJ-length ≤ 3' cusp region in the unit tangent bundle; compare with the count |L₃(p)| ≈ log²p to see the scale.
refs: Strömbergsson, On the uniform equidistribution of long closed horocycles (Duke 2004)

title: Conway topograph of the binary form attached to a word
connection: Each word gives SL₂ data γ_w = [[A,p],[t,A*]] and hence binary quadratic forms (e.g. the form fixed by γ_w, discriminant (A+A*)² − 4). The topograph shows values on the Farey tree and the 'river' for indefinite forms.
why: Conway's topograph turns representation questions into tree navigation, and ES might become 'a value p appears on a well at depth 3 with prescribed sign'.
first_step: For p < 500 draw topographs of the forms fixed by γ_w; look for a common location of p and the sign.

title: Closed geodesic of γ_w on the modular surface: trace N−m and word length 3
connection: γ_w is hyperbolic when |A+A*| > 2. Its closed geodesic has a cutting sequence of length governed by the word. Prime geodesic theorems with Jacobi-symbol twists (Sarnak's class-number sums) count such objects.
why: Prime geodesic theorems in conjugacy classes and with characters are fully developed; ES₅ is a twisted count of geodesics with very short cutting sequences.
first_step: Write trace(γ_w) = tu + tv − 2 = A + A* and list the conjugacy classes; check whether ES₅ is equivalent to a short-cutting-sequence geodesic of trace in a given set with a character condition.
refs: Sarnak, Class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms (1982)

title: U_n as a Looijenga pair: Gross–Hacking–Keel theta functions on the ES log CY surface
connection: The projective closure 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) minus the triangle w = 0 is a log Calabi–Yau surface with a toric model: P² blown up at three collinear boundary points (GEOMETRY_ES Prop 2.1). GHK construct a canonical basis of theta functions on the mirror family of any Looijenga pair, indexed by integral points of the tropicalisation.
why: Theta functions give canonical regular functions with positive structure constants. If positive integer points of U_n correspond to positivity of some theta function's values, the native existence tools are scattering diagrams.
first_step: Compute the scattering diagram of the Looijenga pair (Y_n, D) (three collinear blow-up points). Check whether ES's special position (collinearity) makes it finite (cluster-type) or infinite.
refs: arXiv:1106.4977 (Gross–Hacking–Keel, Mirror symmetry for log Calabi–Yau surfaces I)

title: A¹-curves on U_n and log Gromov–Witten counts vs polynomial ES identities
connection: GHK's theta functions are built from counts of A¹-curves (log GW invariants) meeting the boundary at one point. Integral A¹-curves in U_n are polynomial parametric families of (signed) solutions, the fixed-n analogue of Mordell identities.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says no polynomial families cover square classes. Log GW counts are an enumerative invariant of the same objects, so they might give a geometric reason for which classes are covered.
first_step: Count low-degree A¹-curves on U_n for a few n by direct polynomial search (deg ≤ 3); compare with the GHK broken-line counts.

title: Harpaz's log K3 surfaces: dP5 minus a pentagon and the frieze variety with coefficient N
connection: Harpaz classified log K3 surfaces with trivial geometric Picard group compactifiable to del Pezzos: dP5 with a boundary pentagon of (−1)-curves, which is the A₂ cluster variety. He proved non-Zariski-density of integral points when the Galois action is trivial. The ES₅ frieze (Ptolemy relations with frozen sides (1,1,1,1,N)) is a one-parameter deformation of this variety.
why: It is the closest proved arithmetic theorem about integral points on the exact variety class carrying ES₅ words, and it shows how Brauer–Manin fails to be the only obstruction there.
first_step: Check whether the N-fibre of the pentagon-with-coefficients variety is again dP5 minus a pentagon (a twisted A₂ cluster variety), and read Harpaz §§4–5 for the non-BM obstruction mechanism.
refs: arXiv:1511.01285 (Harpaz, Geometry and arithmetic of certain log K3 surfaces)

title: Integral points on conic log K3 surfaces (Harpaz) applied to the x-fibration of U_n
connection: Fixing x, U_n becomes the hyperbola (ay−b)(az−b) = b² with a = 4x−n, b = nx: a conic bundle over the x-line with split fibres. Harpaz studies integral points on conic-bundle log K3 surfaces.
why: It gives the fibration-method native setting for the classical Type I/II reduction, with a theorem-level description of when integral points exist on such surfaces.
first_step: Read arXiv:1511.04876 and check whether U_n fits its hypotheses (degenerate fibres, boundary). If so, record which part of its existence statement fails to give fibrewise positivity.
refs: arXiv:1511.04876 (Harpaz, Integral points on conic log K3 surfaces)

title: Frieze patterns with coefficients (Cuntz–Holm–Jørgensen) for boundary (1,1,1,1,N)
connection: CHJ develop friezes with coefficients and prove finiteness: for given boundary there are finitely many friezes with entries in a discrete set. They also obtain them by cutting subpolygons out of triangulated polygons. ES₅ words are exactly the positive integral friezes of the pentagon with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) (FRIEZE_ES).
why: Their 'cutting out subpolygons from Conway–Coxeter friezes' construction could realise each ES₅ word inside a classical triangulation of an (N+…)-gon, giving a triangulation model of the sign.
first_step: Read arXiv:1909.02332 §§3–5. Represent each word for p < 200 as a cut-out from a Conway–Coxeter frieze and check whether the sign (4 | quiddity entry) is visible on the triangulation.

title: Conway–Coxeter triangulation count with a mod-4 marked quiddity entry
connection: Classical friezes ↔ triangulations (Conway–Coxeter). The slot lemma says the ES sign is −1 iff 4 divides one of the five pentagon entries (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1). So ES₅ asks for a frieze with coefficients having an entry ≡ 0 (mod 4).
why: 'Some quiddity entry ≡ 0 mod 4' is a reduction-mod-4 condition, and friezes over ℤ/4 (or SL₂(ℤ/4) Farey complexes) are finite objects with full classifications.
first_step: Enumerate the mod-4 reductions of all positive words for p < 10⁵ and record which mod-4 frieze types occur per p; compare with Morier-Genoud's counts of friezes over finite rings.
refs: Morier-Genoud, Counting Coxeter's friezes over a finite field via moduli spaces (check arXiv id)

title: Lyness 5-cycle with a coefficient: integrable map whose integer orbits are ES₅ words
connection: The pentagon Ptolemy relations with one frozen side N give a period-5 birational map (a Lyness-type recurrence x_{k+1}x_{k−1} = x_k + c_k with c ∈ {1,N}). Integer orbits are words. Lyness maps have an invariant cubic (elliptic) fibration.
why: Discrete integrable systems give invariants and elliptic fibrations of such maps; the invariant of the coefficient-N Lyness cycle gives each word a 'conserved energy', possibly with arithmetic meaning.
first_step: Compute the invariant rational function of the (1,1,1,1,N) Lyness cycle (sympy). Evaluate it on words and look for a link with the sign or with t.

title: Tropical frieze / tropicalisation of the pentagon-with-coefficient
connection: Replacing (×,+) by (+,max) gives a tropical frieze: 2-adic or 4-adic valuations of the pentagon entries satisfy tropical Ptolemy relations. The slot lemma condition is a 2-adic valuation event (v₂(entry) ≥ 2).
why: Tropical friezes are piecewise-linear and fully classifiable, so they might give a necessary-and-sufficient 2-adic shape of sign-(−1) words.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation vectors (v₂ of the 5 entries) of all words for p < 10⁵ and the allowed tropical patterns; check whether every p has a pattern with some v₂ ≥ 2.

title: Laurent phenomenon: all frieze entries as Laurent polynomials in an initial seed (c, m) with coefficient N
connection: In a cluster algebra with frozen N, every entry is a Laurent polynomial in an initial cluster. ES words are integrality (positivity) points of these Laurent polynomials, so ES₅ is an 'integer specialisation of a cluster algebra' problem.
why: The theory of integer points of cluster varieties (positivity, theta bases, Fock–Goncharov) is native here, and may give parametrisations of all words by a seed.
first_step: Write the five entries as Laurent polynomials in (c,m) with N; the integrality condition is (cm−1) | (N + c). Record that the frieze reproduces the hyperbola/divisor condition, and check whether any other seed gives a different divisor condition.

title: SL₂-tilings (Bergeron–Reutenauer) containing a row of five with boundary N
connection: SL₂-tilings are infinite arrays of 2×2 minors 1; friezes are bounded tilings. A word gives a finite SL₂-pattern; Bergeron–Reutenauer parametrise tilings by bi-infinite paths in the Farey graph.
why: It turns words into Farey-graph path pairs, where the ES sign might be a holonomy in SL₂(ℤ/4) along the path pair (SVZ already looked at mod-4 contractibility).
first_step: Compute the Bergeron–Reutenauer path pair of each word; check whether the mod-4 holonomy distinguishes signs.
refs: Bergeron–Reutenauer, SL_k-tilings of the plane (Illinois J. 2010)

title: Positive points of cluster varieties ↔ tropical points (Fock–Goncharov duality) for the ES frieze
connection: Fock–Goncharov: positive-integer tropical points of a cluster X-variety parametrise a canonical basis of the dual A-variety. ES words are positive integer points of an A-type frieze variety with coefficient.
why: If ES words were tropical points of a dual variety, existence would become 'a certain polyhedral cone contains an integer point', which is linear.
first_step: Identify the dual (X-variety) of the A₂-with-coefficient frieze variety; compute its tropical points relevant to N; check whether the A-integer points (words) are in bijection with them.
refs: Fock–Goncharov, Cluster ensembles, quantization and the dilogarithm (2009)

title: Quiver representations of A₂ with dimension-vector data equal to a word
connection: Friezes of type A_n categorify via Caldero–Chapoton maps on cluster categories of A_n. Frieze entries are Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians. Coefficients correspond to frozen vertices (Frobenius categories).
why: Categorification gives representation-theoretic meaning to every entry, so 'entry ≡ 0 mod 4' becomes 'Euler characteristic of a quiver Grassmannian ≡ 0 mod 4'.
first_step: Find the Frobenius 2-CY category categorifying friezes with coefficients (Holm–Jørgensen line of work), and identify which objects give entries t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1.

title: Integral points on log CY surfaces: counting conjecture of order (log B)^k and the U_n fibre
connection: For log K3/log CY surfaces the expected integral point count up to height B is a power of log B (Harpaz; Wilsch-type works on integral points of bounded height). U_n has finitely many positive points, but its signed integral points can be counted.
why: The ES expected count ≍ log²n matches 'log-power' heuristics for log CY. Translating the n-dependence into height may connect ES's count to a Manin-type conjecture for integral points.
first_step: Count signed integral points on U_n of height ≤ B for fixed n and growing B (numerically); compare with a (log B)^b law and identify b with the boundary's dual-complex dimension.
refs: Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold (check arXiv)

title: Total family U → A¹_n: integral points on a threefold and Manin–Peyre for the total space
connection: The total space 𝒰 = {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a threefold. ES says the projection 𝒰(ℤ_{>0}) → ℤ_{≥2} is surjective. Integral points on the threefold are counted asymptotically (Elsholtz–Tao averages), so surjectivity is a 'fibre-wise' strengthening.
why: This is the standard 'surjectivity of a morphism on integral points' question, related to Serre's thin-set / Hilbert irreducibility for integral points. The fibres here are log CY rather than rational curves.
first_step: Look up results on 'integral points: surjectivity onto the base' (e.g. Corvaja–Zannier thin sets, integral Hilbert irreducibility) to locate the nearest theorem.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On the Hilbert property and the fundamental group (check)

title: The pencil S_{n,k}: 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = k as a K3-type family with a singular fibre at k = 0
connection: Z52 proved a BM obstruction for k = m² (with congruence conditions) that dies at k = 0. In degeneration theory, the k = 0 fibre is the central fibre of a family of affine cubic surfaces. Brauer classes can extend over the family or ramify at k = 0.
why: Specialisation of Brauer classes in families (purity/residue maps) is a native tool. The residue along the exceptional conic was computed; nearby fibres give limiting information.
first_step: Compute Br of the generic fibre of the pencil over Q(k), and the residues at k = 0 and k = ∞; record whether any class survives as an unramified class on the k = 0 fibre's resolution.

title: Cubic surface 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) as a Cayley-type nodal cubic: Heath-Brown's Cayley cubic counting
connection: The projective closure is a singular cubic surface. Its singularity type (nodes) places it near Cayley's cubic, whose rational point count was computed by Heath-Brown and de la Bretèche via torsor parametrisations.
why: Universal torsors linearise rational points on singular cubics. An integral-point analogue (torsors over the log pair) could parametrise ES solutions by lattice points in a region.
first_step: Determine the singularity type of the closure (via sympy). If it is a 4A₁ Cayley cubic, write its universal torsor and the integral-points condition in torsor coordinates.
refs: Heath-Brown, The density of rational points on Cayley's cubic surface (2003)

title: Integral points via the universal torsor: ES as lattice points satisfying a system of coprime divisibilities
connection: Torsor descent turns 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) into the classical parametrisation x = abd·…, which has the shape of ET's (a,b,c,d) Type I/II data. Torsor coordinates are the standard native coordinates.
why: It explains the ET parametrisations as torsor coordinates, and opens the use of the torsor's own symmetry group, a torus.
first_step: Match ET (2.1)–(2.7) with the Cox ring of the minimal desingularisation of the closure; list any extra torus action not used so far.
refs: Derenthal, Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces (check)

title: Integral Hasse principle for U_n relative to a group action at infinity (ℝ⁺ component)
connection: BL treat the positive real component U_n(ℝ)⁺. In semi-algebraic/o-minimal language, positivity of solutions is an archimedean condition that BM cannot see. Strong approximation with an archimedean constraint is studied for homogeneous spaces.
why: The repo's T1 is a reciprocity obstruction coupling the archimedean and finite places. The native tool is a 'Brauer–Manin with archimedean condition' (BL's U(ℝ)⁺ version).
first_step: Re-read BL §§5–7 for the exact role of U_n(ℝ)⁺; record which Brauer classes have non-constant evaluation on U_n(ℝ)⁺.

title: S-integral ES: denominators allowed at a fixed finite set S of primes
connection: 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ[1/S]_{>0}. For S ∋ 2 this is much easier (more freedom). The ladder S = ∅ ⊂ {2} ⊂ {2,3} ⊂ … is the native 'S-integral points' relaxation of arithmetic geometry.
why: S-integral points on log CY surfaces are much more abundant, and the threshold S where ES becomes provable is a calibration point for the integral question.
first_step: Prove or test ES over ℤ[1/2] (likely an easy covering) and ℤ[1/q] for odd q; compute the minimal S making a finite covering work.

title: ES over number fields with unit-rank ≥ 1 (unit orbits as infinite families)
connection: Over O_K with infinite unit group, U_n(O_K) may have unit-orbit families. UNIT_ORBIT_ES studied these; the native field is Diophantine equations over rings of integers (unit equations, S-unit theorems).
why: Shows what infinite symmetry does to the problem. The S-unit equation theory (Evertse–Győry) gives finiteness or infinitude results for the related unit equations.
first_step: Check whether some ES equivalent form is an S-unit equation in disguise (e.g. after fixing a factorisation pattern) and apply the S-unit counting bounds.
refs: Evertse–Győry, Unit Equations in Diophantine Number Theory (2015)

title: Cubic polynomial T²(T − s) + e(T − n/4) with three positive integer roots
connection: x,y,z are the roots of T³ − sT² + e₂T − e₃ with 4e₃ = n·e₂, i.e. of 4T²(T−s) + e₂(4T − n). So ES(n) ⇔ for some (s, e₂) this cubic splits completely over ℤ with positive roots.
why: It is a 'totally split specialisation' problem for a 2-parameter family of cubics. Hilbert-irreducibility counting and 'polynomials with many split values' (Schinzel-type) are the native field.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(s,e) (generic S₃) and the discriminant surface. Check whether split points lie on a subvariety with a parametrisation (they should be exactly U_n).

title: Elliptic fibration of the ES cubic by planes x + y + z = s
connection: Intersecting the projective closure with the pencil of planes x + y + z = sw gives plane cubic curves, an elliptic fibration (after base-point blow-ups). ES points are integral points on these elliptic curves with positive coordinates.
why: The elliptic-curve toolbox applies fibrewise: Mordell–Weil ranks, Néron–Tate heights and integral points. Ranks along the family could produce infinitely many signed points.
first_step: Compute the Weierstrass model of the s-fibre for fixed n (sympy), and the Mordell–Weil rank of the generic fibre over Q(s).

title: Conic bundle over the x-line: Châtelet-surface toolbox (descent, Schinzel's hypothesis)
connection: The x-fibration is a conic bundle with split degenerate fibres. Châtelet surfaces and conic bundles have Hasse principle results conditional on Schinzel's hypothesis (Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc–Swinnerton-Dyer) and unconditional ones in some degrees (Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov).
why: It is the canonical way the field produces points fibrewise. Integral and positivity constraints are what is missing, but the fibration method with additive combinatorics (Green–Tao input) is a powerful modern variant.
first_step: Write the x-fibration's degenerate fibres as linear forms in x. Check whether Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov's linear-forms setting applies to integral points with x in a short range.
refs: Browning–Matthiesen–Skorobogatov, Rational points on pencils of conics and quadrics with many degenerate fibres (Ann. Math. 2014)

title: Vojta/abc for integral points on U_n: what does 'log Kodaira dimension 0' predict
connection: Vojta's conjecture predicts degeneracy of integral points only for log general type. U_n is log CY (κ̄ = 0), so integral points may be dense, and no prediction of existence follows.
why: This is a calibration: it explains why no conjectural Diophantine machine gives ES, unlike Markoff (log CY too) where Ghosh–Sarnak found failures.
first_step: Note as calibration. Check whether 'log CY with BM set non-empty but positive points absent' is known to occur infinitely often in a family (Loughran–Mitankin for Markoff).
refs: Loughran–Mitankin, Integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for Markoff surfaces (IMRN 2021; check)

title: Arakelov/height view: ES solutions have height ≤ n³-type bound, a Π⁰₁ statement
connection: Positive solutions satisfy x ≤ 3n/4, y ≤ n²-ish and z ≤ n⁴-ish (Curtiss-type bounds), so ES is a Π⁰₁ arithmetic sentence. Heights in Arakelov theory bound points; existence of small-height points is a Siegel-lemma question.
why: Siegel's lemma or geometry of numbers on the torsor might produce small points if a linear structure is present (e.g. Type II at fixed C is linear in some coordinates).
first_step: State precisely the height bounds for positive solutions. Check whether any linear sub-system at fixed (C,d) has a Siegel-lemma solution of the right size.

title: Toric degeneration of U_n to the torus complement xyz ≠ 0 and the Newton polytope
connection: As n varies, 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) degenerates (n → 0, n → ∞) to toric strata. Newton polytope methods (Bernstein–Kushnirenko, Khovanskii) count solutions in tori over finite fields; positive integer solutions relate to the polytope's interior lattice points.
why: Newton-polytope/tropical methods give exact solution counts over F_q (Ax–Katz divisibility of point counts) and might give mod-2 parity of solution counts.
first_step: Compute #U_n(F_q) exactly via the toric model and check Ax–Katz-type q-divisibility; record whether any parity information survives to positive integer points.

title: Motivic/Igusa zeta function of U_n: local densities and the BM main term
connection: The BM main term is a product of local densities, each the limit of #U_n(ℤ/p^k)/p^{2k}. Igusa's local zeta function encodes these densities as rational functions with poles governed by an embedded resolution.
why: The exact local factors (especially at 2) control the T1/sign phenomena. Igusa poles might give a uniform closed form for the BM constant, which is already exact.
first_step: Compute Igusa zeta of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at p = 2 and p | n via the toric resolution; compare with BM_CORRECTED_COUNT local factors.

title: Hasse principle for the 'Type II at fixed level' variety: d | 4Cn+1, d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) as a norm-form/torus variety
connection: At fixed C, a solution is a factorisation 4Cn+1 = d·d′ with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C). This is an integral point on a torus-type variety (norm form for the trivial extension, with level structure). Ray-class-field reciprocity says the class of d is constrained.
why: Torus-variety integral points with level structure are governed by class field theory (ray class groups). ES at fixed C is exactly a ray-class question, B2.
first_step: Record the ray class group mod 4C whose Frobenius class decides it, and the explicit list of p's covered for C ≤ 20 (sanity link to Mordell covering).

title: Integral points on the affine quadric family: Type I as a sum-of-squares/norm condition in ℤ[√−d]
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.1: Type I at level d ⇔ (1+2aw)(1+2bw) = e(2cw − p) in ℤ[w], w = √−d. This is a factorisation problem in an imaginary quadratic order.
why: Factorisation in quadratic orders is governed by the class group and genus theory, and the repo uses it in LATTICE_MEETING. The native next step is a Heegner-point/CM-points equidistribution input.
first_step: Express the condition as 'a specific ideal of norm e lies in a class of order ≤ 2·something'; test which genus characters are forced.

title: Bhargava cubes: the Type II cube point (c,d,j) as a 2×2×2 integer cube
connection: FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS packages Type II data as a cube point; Bhargava's cube law composes three binary quadratic forms. If certificates are cubes with a fixed corner, composition gives relations among certificates of different n.
why: Bhargava's parametrisations come with orbit-counting (geometry of numbers on prehomogeneous spaces), which gives averages but sometimes also exact class-group relations.
first_step: Write a certificate as an explicit 2×2×2 cube and compute its three binary forms; check which one has discriminant related to p and what composition does to certificates.
refs: Bhargava, Higher composition laws I (Ann. Math. 2004)

title: Prehomogeneous vector space view: averages are easy, pointwise is the problem (calibration)
connection: Orbit-counting on prehomogeneous spaces gives averages over discriminants (Davenport–Heilbronn style). ES's averages are known (Vaughan, ET), and the pointwise question has no prehomogeneous analogue.
why: This calibrates what arithmetic statistics can give: possibly a positive-proportion statement in the n-aspect with explicit constants, not ES.
first_step: Skip unless a pointwise parametrisation arises. Note as a calibration entry.

title: Lenstra's 'divisors in residue classes' bound applied to 4Cp+1
connection: Lenstra (1984): if s > N^{1/3} and gcd(r,s) = 1, there are at most 11 divisors of N congruent to r mod s, all found in polynomial time (via Coppersmith-type lattice methods). ES Type II asks for a divisor of N = 4Cp+1 in the class −1 mod 4C, with 4C ≪ N^{1/2}.
why: It is the algorithmic-number-theory native statement about exactly this object. It gives upper bounds and fast search, never existence, which calibrates where existence must come from.
first_step: Read Hales arXiv:2410.05030 (Divisors in residue classes revisited) for the current best constants; note the regime s ≈ N^{1/2} vs ES's s ≈ N^{small}.
refs: Lenstra, Divisors in residue classes, Math. Comp. 42 (1984)

title: Coppersmith small-root method: find (d, d′) with dd′ = 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a small root of a bivariate polynomial
connection: Writing d = 4Ck − 1 makes the condition (4Ck−1)·d′ = 4Cp+1, a bivariate polynomial with a small root (k, d′). Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham finds small roots when they exist below a size bound.
why: This is the crypto-native 'factoring with a hint' toolbox. A lattice whose reduced basis has a short vector exactly when a certificate exists would be an existence criterion of a new kind (a Minkowski bound).
first_step: Build the Howgrave-Graham lattice for fixed small C and p ~ 10¹²; check whether the reduced-basis norm predicts certificate existence (compare with ground truth).

title: Modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 (mod p) with X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (mod t) and XY = tp+1
connection: Words ↔ points (X,Y) = (A, A*) on the modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 mod p with X, Y ≡ −1 mod t and the exact archimedean condition XY = tp+1. Shparlinski's survey covers point counts in boxes via Kloosterman sums.
why: Native results give points of XY ≡ c mod m in boxes of side ≥ m^{1/2+ε}. ES needs a hyperbola-shaped region (XY exactly tp+1), and that shape is the whole difficulty.
first_step: From Shparlinski's survey, locate the best result on modular-hyperbola points in hyperbolic (not box) regions and see what size it requires.

title: Hooley's Δ / Erdős–Hall–Tenenbaum divisor concentration for N_t = tp+1
connection: ES₅ at level t needs a divisor of N_t = tp+1 in the class −1 mod t in a prescribed size window. Divisor-concentration functions (Hooley's Δ, Ford's H(x,y,2y)) measure how often integers have divisors in short intervals.
why: These are the probabilistic-NT tools for 'some divisor of N lands in a window'. Here the window is a residue class rather than an interval, so it needs a twisted Δ.
first_step: Define Δ_t(N) = max over residue-class windows; compute its distribution for N_t, p < 10⁷, against random integers.
refs: Ford, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval (Ann. Math. 2008)

title: Titchmarsh divisor problem with congruence: Σ_{p≤x} #{d | p+a : d ≡ r mod q}
connection: Summing ES certificate counts over p is a Titchmarsh-type divisor problem in progressions (Fouvry, Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec). It controls averages and exceptional sets, as LORENZINI_W used Linnik/Halberstam.
why: This is the native average tool, already in the repo; recorded so the map is complete. BFI-level distribution beyond 1/2 could improve exceptional-set exponents.
first_step: Check whether BFI's level-4/7 results apply to the specific moduli 4C with the −1 class; if so, compute the resulting exceptional-set exponent.

title: Semi-linear / half-dimensional sieve for 'some divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'
connection: The condition that N has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4 (or in a class) is a half-dimensional sieve problem (Iwaniec's semi-linear sieve). Integers with all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4C fail.
why: The half-dimensional sieve gives sharp lower bounds for 'no prime factor in a class' sets. ES's certificate failure at fixed C is such a set, intersected over C.
first_step: Write the failure at fixed C as 'all divisors avoid −1 mod 4C' (stronger than a prime-factor condition); quantify with the half-dimensional sieve over C ≤ log p and check the expected joint-failure density.
refs: Iwaniec, The half dimensional sieve (Acta Arith. 1976)

title: Multiplicative subgroup generated by prime factors: Frobenius / Chebotarev form of 'divisor in coset'
connection: A divisor d of N in the class −1 mod 4C exists iff a subset product of the prime factors of N hits −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×. This is a zero-sum / subset-product problem in a finite abelian group (Davenport constant).
why: The Davenport constant D(G) says any sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence. Subset-product hitting −1 needs ω(N) about D((ℤ/4C)^×) primes in general position.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and C ≤ 30, compute ω(4Cp+1) and whether the prime classes' subset products cover −1; compare with Davenport-constant thresholds.

title: Olson/Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv-type theorem for 'subset product = −1' in (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Zero-sum theory has inverse theorems: sequences with no zero-sum subsequence are structured (lie in a coset). ES failure at fixed C forces the prime factors of 4Cp+1 to lie in an index-2-type structure that avoids −1.
why: Inverse zero-sum theorems give explicit structure of failing configurations, which is a different angle from sieve counting.
first_step: State: the subset products of ω primes avoid −1 ⇒ all lie in a subgroup H not containing −1 or the configuration is short. Check against data for p < 10⁶.
refs: Gao–Geroldinger survey, Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups (2006)

title: Least prime in an arithmetic progression (Linnik) vs least certificate level
connection: ES certificates at level C are prime-free (divisors, not primes), but the simplest certificates use a prime q ≡ 3 mod 4 with (p/q) = −1 or similar. Linnik's constant controls the least such prime.
why: The least-QNR and Linnik problems are the archetypal 'pointwise thin existence' theorems in NT, and the repo uses Burgess for the BM main term.
first_step: Calibration: compare least ES certificate level with ℓ(p) (least prime with (p/ℓ) = −1) for p ≤ 10⁹; is the certificate level ≤ C·ℓ(p)^κ?

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture as a sufficient hypothesis for the BM layer only
connection: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9: the BM layer is pointwise free, i.e. some level 4 | t ≤ 4ℓ(p) has a positive main term. The remaining question is the class of the divisor inside a coset. Least-QNR bounds control the first layer only.
why: This calibrates what 'standard conjectures' buy; the second layer needs a different hypothesis (equidistribution of divisor classes of one integer).
first_step: Formulate the minimal second-layer hypothesis ('divisors of tp+1 equidistribute in (ℤ/t)^× for some t ≤ T') and compare it with the known Erdős–Hall/Montgomery-type results on divisor class distribution.

title: Divisors of a single integer equidistributing in residue classes (Montgomery/Erdős–Hall for one N)
connection: For one integer N with many prime factors, its divisors equidistribute mod q under mild hypotheses (a Fourier / random-walk argument on (ℤ/q)^×). ES needs this for N = 4Cp+1, which typically has few (~log log p) factors.
why: It is the native single-integer statement. Its failure mode (few prime factors) is exactly why ES is hard; the field has results for 'typical' N only.
first_step: Quantify: for N with ω(N) = k primes in random classes mod q, P(no divisor ≡ −1) ≈ ? (subset-product random walk). Compare with observed per-level failure.

title: Random walks on (ℤ/q)^× generated by prime factors: cutoff and mixing of subset products
connection: Subset products of k random elements of an abelian group G cover G once k ≳ log|G| (Erdős–Rényi random subset products). ES wants −1 covered with k ≈ log log p generators: a 'pre-cutoff' regime.
why: Random-walk theory is precise about pre-cutoff probabilities; combined across many levels C it gives a heuristic failure probability.
first_step: Compute P(−1 ∈ subset-products) for k random elements of (ℤ/4C)^× by exact enumeration; plug into a Poisson model over C ≤ C₀.
refs: Erdős–Rényi, Probabilistic methods in group theory (1965)

title: Kloosterman-sum form of the word count R_t(p) and Weil-bound positivity
connection: #{(X,Y): XY = tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t), sizes} is a divisor-in-progression count. Its sign-twisted version Σ(A/p) is a sum of Jacobi symbols over divisors, expressible by Kloosterman/Salié sums after Poisson summation.
why: Weil's bound is the native positivity tool. It needs long sums, and the word count per level is O(1), which is the B3 issue in native terms.
first_step: Write the χ-twisted level-t count as a Salié sum expression and record the length vs modulus ratio.

title: Bilinear forms in Kloosterman sums (Kowalski–Michel–Sawin) for the sum over levels t
connection: Summing over levels t ≤ T and divisors gives a bilinear form in Kloosterman-type sums. KMS proved non-trivial bounds for bilinear Kloosterman forms below the Pólya–Vinogradov range.
why: It is the strongest modern native tool for sub-Pólya–Vinogradov cancellation in exactly this kind of sum. It might give cancellation in the sign-twisted total ΣN₋ − N₊ over many levels.
first_step: Write N₊ − N₋ summed over t ≤ T as Σ_t Σ_{m} α_t β_m Kl(…; p) and check the KMS hypotheses (ranges M, N vs p^{1/2}).
refs: Kowalski–Michel–Sawin, Bilinear forms with Kloosterman sums (Ann. Math. 2017)

title: Burgess-type bounds for character sums over 'divisor sets' (multiplicative structure)
connection: ES₅ needs χ_p to be non-constant on S₃(p) = {A : r(p/A) = 3}, a set of size ≈ log²p built from divisors. Character sums over multiplicatively structured sets (products of two sets) admit Burgess/bilinear bounds.
why: S₃(p) = {(p+u)/v : v | p+u, …}: if it contains a product set A·B mod p with |A|,|B| ≫ p^ε, bilinear character-sum bounds would force a non-residue.
first_step: Check computationally whether S₃(p) (or the larger S_L(p)) contains large product sets A·B mod p.

title: Sum-product / Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin for the set S_L(p) as L grows
connection: S_L(p) = {A : r(p/A) ≤ L} grows like p^{c(L)} for L ≫ log p. Sum-product theory says sets of size p^δ generate F_p in bounded steps. ES₅ fixes L = 3, where |S₃| ≈ log²p.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics frame for why L = 3 is hard (polylog sets have no sum-product leverage) and where L-ladders become easy.
first_step: Tabulate |S_L(p)| and the least L with S_L(p) ⊄ QR for p < 10⁶ (this is λ(p)); fit L_min growth.

title: Zaremba-type pointwise theorem for HJ continued fractions with bounded length instead of bounded digits
connection: Zaremba (Bourgain–Kontorovich; claimed in full by Zhang 2605.02518) bounds digits; ES₅ bounds length with unbounded digits. The 'dual Zaremba' problem, existence of A with r(p/A) ≤ L in a prescribed coset, is the ES form.
why: The thin-orbit machinery is the nearest proved pointwise theory. Its failure here (fixed length means no expansion) is known, but the dual formulation is native to Larcher/Chang-type results on short CF.
first_step: Look up results on 'continued fractions of bounded length/sum of partial quotients' modulo p (Chang Thm 5, Larcher) and whether any includes a character condition.

title: McMullen's uniformly diophantine numbers in a fixed quadratic field ↔ periodic HJ data
connection: McMullen showed every real quadratic field contains infinitely many periodic continued fractions with bounded partial quotients. ES words relate to quadratic data via γ_w (trace A + A*). A quadratic-field-uniform statement is a model for 'certificates in every class'.
why: It is one of the rare pointwise CF theorems proved by a non-expansion argument (closed geodesics, Hecke-type operators).
first_step: Read McMullen 'Uniformly Diophantine numbers in a fixed real quadratic field' (Compositio 2009) and check whether its geodesic-construction trick could prescribe a trace/level relation like ES's.
refs: McMullen, Uniformly Diophantine numbers in a fixed real quadratic field (Compos. Math. 2009)

title: Rickards–Stange reciprocity obstruction as the model of T1
connection: RS prove semigroup orbits in SL₂(ℤ) can miss squares through a reciprocity obstruction (Jacobi symbols on the orbit), with finitely many sporadic exceptions in the 'fat' case. QUESTION_R casts ES as such a thin orbit with T1 as the reciprocity obstruction.
why: It is the nearest proved local-global-with-reciprocity theorem. The native next step is to place ES₅/U(n) inside an RS-type semigroup.
first_step: Already pursued (QUESTION_R). Here: check whether U(n)'s six sporadics fit an RS 'sporadic set' pattern (e.g. explained by a finite-index sub-orbit).

title: Apollonian local-global failures (Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange) as precedent for sporadic lists
connection: HKRS disproved the Apollonian local-global conjecture via quadratic and quartic reciprocity obstructions. ES's T1 is a quadratic-reciprocity obstruction at squares; a 'quartic' analogue might predict new ES-like missing families in variants.
why: It shows how reciprocity obstructions are found and proved in thin orbits. A quartic-reciprocity obstruction in an ES variant (e.g. U(n)) would explain its sporadics.
first_step: Test U(n) failures and the ES variants (ES₅, I3_𝒞) for quartic-residue patterns (n ≡ fourth powers × units, or quartic symbols at 2).
refs: Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false (check arXiv id)

title: Hidden Number Problem formulation: recover/obtain A from partial information on A·x mod p
connection: Boneh–Venkatesan's HNP finds α from approximations of α·t_i mod p. The ES₅ condition r(p/A) = 3 says A/p lies near 1/v with a prescribed error structure (A = (p+u)/v), an approximation statement about A mod p.
why: HNP and lattice-reduction tools are native for 'find an element mod p with given approximate multiples'. Reversing them (choose A with small multiples) is a geometry-of-numbers existence question.
first_step: Write the ES₅ word condition as 'vA ≡ u (mod p) with uv small, (u,v) in a hyperbolic region'; check the Minkowski bound for the lattice {(x, y) : y ≡ Ax mod p} restricted to non-residue A.

title: The lattice Λ_A = {(x,y) : y ≡ Ax (mod p)}: ES₅ ⇔ a non-residue A whose lattice has a short vector in a hyperbolic region
connection: vA ≡ u (mod p) with v | p+u means (v, u) ∈ Λ_A with uv small. By Minkowski every Λ_A has a vector with |x||y| ≤ p. ES₅ needs (v, u) with vA − u = p exactly (not just mod p) and positive.
why: It is geometry of numbers in its native form: minima of the family of lattices Λ_A over A ∈ QNR. Successive minima of Λ_A relate to CF data, with a Hecke-type averaging over A.
first_step: For p < 10⁵ compute λ₁(Λ_A) for all A and the minimum over non-residue A of the product-norm minimum; relate to λ(p).

title: Klein polygons / sails of the cone for p/A: HJ length = number of sail vertices
connection: The HJ continued fraction of p/A is read off the boundary of the convex hull of lattice points in the cone spanned by (1,0) and (A,p) (Klein's sail). r(p/A) = 3 means the sail has a fixed small number of vertices.
why: Arnold's statistics of sails and multidimensional continued fractions are a native toolbox. Sails with few vertices are rare and structured.
first_step: Express 'sail of cone(p,A) has 3 interior vertices' and count over A ∈ QNR; compare with Arnold's predictions for random cones.

title: Vallée's dynamical analysis of Euclidean algorithms (by-excess algorithm) with a quadratic character
connection: The HJ expansion is the 'by-excess' Euclidean algorithm. Vallée's transfer-operator method gives limit laws for costs such as length. ES₅ asks for the extreme value: min length over A in the non-residue class equals 3.
why: It is the native analysis-of-algorithms framework; twisting transfer operators by Dirichlet characters is done in Baladi–Vallée-type works.
first_step: Look up whether the by-excess algorithm's length distribution has been studied with a character twist (Baladi–Vallée 2005 for Gauss map; Dolgopyat estimates).

title: Rényi (backward CF) map x ↦ 1/(1−x) − ⌊⋯⌋: infinite invariant measure and orbit length 3
connection: The HJ expansion is generated by the Rényi map, whose invariant measure dx/x is infinite (parabolic fixed point). Short orbits from A/p to 0 in 3 steps are the ES₅ words.
why: Infinite-ergodic-theory tools (Aaronson, Thaler) describe return statistics near the parabolic point, and ES words are 'fast escapes', the complementary regime.
first_step: Compute the measure of points with exactly 3-step Rényi orbits to the cusp at resolution 1/p; compare with |L₃(p)|/p.
refs: Aaronson, An Introduction to Infinite Ergodic Theory (1997)

title: Mayer/Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing transfer operator twisted by (·/p): spectral gap for character sums over CF sets
connection: Character sums over sets defined by CF conditions can be studied by transfer operators with a character twist (as in Bourgain–Kontorovich and Dolgopyat). A spectral gap gives cancellation in Σ_{A: CF condition} χ(A).
why: It is the native way to get cancellation for CF-defined sets, but works for growing lengths, not length 3. Recorded as the nearest tool.
first_step: Record the length threshold L(p) beyond which twisted transfer-operator methods give non-trivial Σ_{A ∈ S_L(p)} (A/p); compare with λ(p) data.
refs: Mayer 1991 (transfer operator of the Gauss map)

title: Farey-fraction spin chain (Kleban–Özlük) partition function and the ES words
connection: Kleban–Özlük's Farey spin chain has a partition function built from products of matrices [[1,0],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[0,1]], and its states are Farey fractions. ES words correspond to specific length-3 HJ blocks, so a restricted partition function counts them.
why: Statistical mechanics of number-theoretic chains has exact phase-transition results; a 'Legendre-field' coupling would make the ES sign a magnetization.
first_step: Define Z_p(β, h) = Σ_{A} e^{−β·r(p/A)} (A/p)^{h}; compute for p < 10⁴ and look at the h-derivative at β → ∞ (the min-length sign).
refs: Kleban–Özlük, A Farey fraction spin chain (CMP 1999)

title: Knauf's number-theoretic spin chain and Riemann ζ: a ζ-like Dirichlet series for HJ lengths
connection: Knauf's spin chain partition function is ζ(s−1)/ζ(s). An analogous chain with HJ (by-excess) matrices and a quadratic-character field might have a Dirichlet-series partition function whose coefficients encode λ(p).
why: If the partition function is an L-function quotient, analytic properties (zeros/poles) would control its coefficients.
first_step: Compute Σ_{p,A} p^{−s} x^{r(p/A)} (A/p) numerically and try to identify it as an L-function combination.
refs: Knauf, On a ferromagnetic spin chain (CMP 1993)

title: Hecke operators on the space of words: does T_ℓ map ES₅ words of p to words of ℓp or ℓ²p?
connection: Hecke operators act on SL₂(ℤ)-cosets/matrices with fixed determinant structure. Words are SL₂ matrices with upper-right entry p. Hecke correspondences relate matrices with entry p to entry ℓp.
why: It is the modular-forms-native way to get relations between different n. A Hecke-equivariant structure on certificates would allow induction.
first_step: Apply the coset representatives of T_2 to γ_w and check which images are words (positive, upper-right p or 4p) and how the sign transforms.
